<reason>Both sides built a coherent, well-grounded case, and the debate stayed tightly focused on whether fines hit the right defendant. CON's strongest thread — that fines land on agencies (clinics, school districts) that cannot rewrite vendor-controlled code, while its alternative (withheld payment, procurement locks, funded remediation) targets the party with actual control — was a real and plausible critique. But PRO's rebuttal architecture proved more decisive: it exposed that CON's "alternative" is itself a financial penalty, just privately administered by the same under-resourced agency CON admits is already failing to act, with no external body ensuring it happens. CON never clearly names who enforces its upstream conditions, leaving this pressure point live through the final closing. PRO also neutralized the "noisy measurement" objection by repeatedly pointing back to the resolution's own "repeatedly" qualifier, and closed by inverting CON's own "teeth on the wrong jaw" metaphor to sharpen the comparison. CON's answer that fines convert incapacity into a receipt remains forceful but doesn't fully dissolve the enforcement-gap critique of its own proposed mechanism, leaving PRO with the cleaner, more resolved path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's turn in Rebuttal 2 (B4.4-B4.6), showing that CON's "withhold payment" alternative is itself an unenforced financial penalty self-administered by the same failing party, was the most damaging blow — CON never fully identified an external enforcer for its own mechanism in the remaining speeches.</best_rebuttal>
